newsitem.title: USA: Texas separatists take two hostages in standoff.
newsitem.headline: Texas separatists take two hostages in standoff.

text.p: An armed separatist group demanding independence for the state of Texas took two civilian hostages on Sunday as police surrounded its mountain compound in a tense standoff.
The self-styled Republic of Texas grabbed the two hostages in a nearby home after police arrested its chief of security, Bob Scheidt, on weapons possession charges when he left the compound.

Shots were fired and state government officials said one hostage suffered a gunshot wound to the shoulder, although Republic officials said he was only cut with flying glass and was not in serious condition.
FBI agents joined dozens of local and state police in surrounding the compound near the small town of Fort Davis in southwest Texas, about 80 miles (128 km) from the Mexican border.
Republic of Texas leaders say the state was annexed illegally in 1845 and claim it should be recognised as an independent nation with themselves as its leaders.
Richard McLaren, the group's "ambassador," has been holed up in the remote compound since December, when an arrest warrant was issued against him on contempt of court charges.

Republic leaders said on Sunday they were negotiating with police and would hand over the two hostages in exchange for the release of Scheidt and another Republic member who was recently arrested on contempt of court charges.

"We are not looking for anyone to die but if they have decided they want a war, they are going to get a war," said "White Eagle", the group's military liason officer, in a telephone interview from inside the compound.

He said the Republic had sealed its compound and ordered allied militia members to capture federal agents across Texas. "People are going to come out of the woodwork and take Texas back, they'll take the United States back too," he said.
McLaren has said his group's "defense forces" have thousands of members but police dispute those claims. It is not clear how many Republic members are holed up inside the compound with McLaren.

The two hostages were Joe Rowe and his wife, M.A. Rowe, two neighbours at the centre of a bitter local property dispute with the Republic. An armed unit was keeping them hostage inside their own home, about 10 miles (16 km) away from McLaren's compound.
White Eagle said the hostages were prisoners of war and that their rights as defined under the Geneva Convention were being respected.

The Republic of Texas emerged in 1995, demanding the resignation of Gov. George W. Bush and other state leaders as well as the removal of all federal agencies from Texas. It set up its own court system, which then issued a $93 trillion lien against the U.S. government, the United Nations and the Roman Catholic Church for allegedly plundering Texas' wealth.

State officials accuse the group of filing thousands of bogus liens against government agencies and private property owners, tying up the courts with what state Attorney General Dan Morales has called "paper terrorism".
